Put these three values in `web/.env` yourself. I will not open that file.

- `GITHUB_APP_ID` — the numeric App ID on the GitHub App settings page
- `GITHUB_APP_SLUG` — the slug in `https://github.com/apps/<slug>`
- `GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` — the app’s PEM private key, with real newlines written as `\n`

On the GitHub App, set the **Setup URL** to `http://localhost:3000/api/github/callback` (use the port you actually run), and turn on **Redirect on update**. Leave **Request user authorization (OAuth) during installation** off. This flow uses the install redirect (`installation_id`), not an OAuth code.

Repository permissions the install needs:

- **Metadata:** Read (GitHub turns this on automatically)
- **Contents:** Read (so private repos can list branches)
- **Pull requests:** Read and write (the agent opens pull requests against the branch you pick)

After you save the env file, tell me the slug, whether the Setup URL is saved, and whether OAuth-during-install is off. The onboarding step already installs the app, lists the repos that install can see, and lets you pick one repository and its branch.

Add these three lines to `web/.env`. The slug comes from your public link, `https://github.com/apps/friction-fixer`.

```
GITHUB_APP_ID=5263576
GITHUB_APP_SLUG=friction-fixer
GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY="paste the .pem here with line breaks written as \n"
```

The private key is not on the page you pasted. On that same GitHub App page, open **Private keys**, click **Generate a private key**, and put the downloaded `.pem` in `GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY`. One line is fine if every real newline is written as `\n`.

Then change one setting on the app. **Setup URL** is `https://friction-fixer.shivamtaneja.com/dashboard`. After install, GitHub sends `installation_id` to that URL, and this app only reads it on the callback.

- Testing on your machine: set **Setup URL** to `http://localhost:3000/api/github/callback`
- Testing on the live site: set **Setup URL** to `https://friction-fixer.shivamtaneja.com/api/github/callback`

Turn on **Redirect on update**. Leave **Request user authorization (OAuth) during installation** off, so GitHub uses the Setup URL. The Redirect URI can stay as it is. You do not need the Client ID or the webhook secret for this step.

what about webhook do i need them? or no? and i have it downloaded. and i've updated the setup url
http://localhost:3000/api/github/callback to this for now
</user_query>
You don’t need a webhook for connecting a repo. I’ll confirm the app never receives one today so that answer stays exact.

No. Leave the webhook off for this step.

Connecting a repository only uses the Setup URL you just set. After install, GitHub redirects the browser to `http://localhost:3000/api/github/callback` with the installation id. The app then asks GitHub for the repos and branches with the private key. Nothing in this app listens at `/api/github/webhook`, so an active webhook has nowhere to land.

On the GitHub App page, uncheck **Active** under Webhook. You can turn it back on later if the app needs events such as a deleted install or a merged pull request.

With the `.pem` downloaded and the Setup URL saved, the only remaining piece is those three lines in `web/.env`: `GITHUB_APP_ID`, `GITHUB_APP_SLUG`, and `GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY`.

<timestamp>Sunday, Oct 11, 2026, 2:59 PM (UTC+5:30)</timestamp>
<user_query>
for my usecase do i need webhook or not?
</user_query>
The connect step does not use a webhook. I’ll check what this product actually does with GitHub after that, so the answer matches your use case.

No. For this product, leave the webhook off.

Friction Fixer calls GitHub: it installs on the one repo you pick, reads that repo, opens a pull request, and reverts that pull request if the change does not help. Those are all requests your app sends, using the private key and the installation from the Setup URL. GitHub does not need to call you back.

A webhook is only for the other direction, when GitHub should notify you that something changed while you were not asking. That would matter later if you want an immediate signal that someone merged the pull request, or removed the app. Until then, the agent can check the pull request itself.

so when connecting i just need to save the tokens so that when i actually work/the agent works it can pull the code from that repo. that's the logic i wnat to do!

Save the installation, the repository, and the branch. Create the GitHub token from those when the agent actually pulls the code.

GitHub's installation token expires after about an hour, so a token stored at connect time will be dead by the time the agent runs. The durable piece is the installation id. Your app private key plus that id produces a fresh token whenever you need one.

On connect, the callback already stores that installation for the signed-in user. When onboarding finishes, the project stores the chosen repository, the branch, and the same installation id. Nothing token-shaped is written to the database.

When the agent runs later, the steps are:

1. Load that user's installation id, repository, and branch.
2. Sign a short-lived app token with `GITHUB_APP_ID` and `GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY`.
3. Exchange it for an installation token.
4. Clone or fetch `owner/repo` with that token and check out the saved branch.

The onboarding step already does steps 2 and 3 when it lists repositories and branches. The Python agent does not use this yet. It still reads a separate `GITHUB_TOKEN` from `agent/.env`.
